title: I celebrate myself
hookLine: a poet opens his book by praising himself, then hands every atom of it to you
tomorrow: a child hands him grass and asks what it is. what does he say?

lines: NO NAME ON THE TITLE PAGE.
cards: A friend posts a birthday carousel, all selfies, captioned main character era, and the group chat goes quiet in that particular way. Too much? Now a print shop in Brooklyn.

A tall man in a work shirt, hat tipped back, is getting his own book of poems ready. No author's name on the title page. Just an engraving of him, collar open, one hand on his hip, like a laborer between jobs.
And the long poem inside begins: "I celebrate myself."

teach.h: EVERY ATOM BELONGS TO YOU AS WELL.
teach.b: It sounds like that carousel, long before phones. In later editions he made the line even bolder: "I celebrate myself, and sing myself."
Then, in the very next breath, Whitman turns it inside out: "And what I assume you shall assume, For every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you." He isn't celebrating himself instead of you.
He's celebrating himself as you: the same atoms, the same breath, the same grass underfoot.
Later he names himself: "Walt Whitman, a kosmos, of Manhattan the son." A kosmos is a whole ordered world. And his I keeps widening.

teach.h: OLD AND YOUNG, FOOLISH AND WISE.
teach.b: "I am of old and young, of the foolish as much as the wise," he says, and he goes on: parent and child, Northerner and Southerner, a boatman on the lakes. That's the teaching of the poem's opening.

teach.h: THE SELF IS A DOOR, NOT A WALL.
teach.b: The self, looked at honestly and loved, isn't a wall around one person. It's a door into everyone. Some readers call it a democratic faith: nobody outside the circle, nobody above it.
So the difference from vanity is the direction. Vanity says: look at me, not you. Whitman says: look at me, and you'll find yourself.

how: Some people on this path read Whitman's Song of Myself aloud, a section at a time, and pause on the lines where his "I" widens to take in everyone.

o: a holiday where poets honor their own work
a vow to put yourself first, before others
praising your own self as part of everyone

games.q: the poem that starts with a self: tap the pairs.
p: a whole world in one man

s: Whitman's 'I celebrate myself' puts himself above everyone else
the next lines turn it: every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you.
the book's title page carried no author's name
just an engraving of a man in a work shirt; his name comes later, inside the poem.
Whitman's 'I' stays one man all through the poem
it keeps widening: old and young, foolish and wise, Northerner and Southerner.

games.q: a friend says Whitman's opening is just ego, the first selfie. what's Whitman's best answer, from the poem itself?
o: the next lines: what I assume you shall assume; every atom of me belongs to you.
he was joking; the poem means the opposite of what it says.
poets get a pass; bragging doesn't count when it's art.
games.why: the poem answers itself in the next breath. the self he praises is the one everyone shares, atom for atom.

practice: Choose one ordinary thing about you: your hands, your laugh, the way you make coffee. Say it out loud, plainly, the way Whitman would: I celebrate my hands.
Then let it widen, quietly: hands like these are working all over the world right now.

wordCard.voice: I celebrate myself: the opening of Whitman's Song of Myself, where praising one ordinary self opens out into everyone, every atom shared.
